rome-seven-hills-tiber-river-winter-morn.head: The Romans did not number their years from a fixed date, but named each year after its two consuls.
rome-seven-hills-tiber-river-winter-morn.body: In ancient Rome, each year was identified by the names of the two consuls, the highest elected officials of the Republic. The year now called 44 before Christ was known in Rome as the year of the consulship of Gaius Julius Caesar and Marcus Antonius. Lists of consuls, called the fasti, were kept carefully and carved in stone, so that Romans could identify past years. Some writers also counted years from the traditional founding of the city, which Romans placed in 753 before Christ. By that system, 44 before Christ was roughly the seven hundred and tenth year of Rome. Historians use the surviving consular lists to date events precisely. Fragments of these lists, called the Fasti Capitolini, are now displayed in the Capitoline Museums. Even so, the dating system used today, counting from the birth of Christ, was devised only in the sixth century after Christ. In the winter of 44 before Christ, Rome was a large and busy city spread across its famous hills.

roof-tiles-frost-smoke-rising-hills-pale.head: Winter in Rome was mild, and people warmed their rooms with small braziers of glowing charcoal.
roof-tiles-frost-smoke-rising-hills-pale.body: Rome lies in central Italy, about fifteen miles from the sea, and its winters are relatively mild. Frost and snow were unusual, though cold winds and heavy rain could make the season uncomfortable. Most Roman homes had no central heating. Wealthy houses sometimes had heated floors, called hypocausts, especially in their baths, but this was rare in ordinary homes. Instead, people used braziers, metal or clay containers filled with burning charcoal, to warm their rooms. They wore extra tunics and thick woollen cloaks. Historians know about Roman heating from archaeological finds, such as braziers excavated at Pompeii and Herculaneum, and from the writings of ancient authors. Braziers were dangerous, because charcoal fumes could be harmful in closed rooms and fires could spread easily. Even so, they were the usual way of keeping warm. On winter mornings, smoke from countless braziers, ovens and lamps rose above the tiled roofs of the city.

forum-valley-temples-basilicas-morning.head: At the centre of Rome lay the Forum, the main public square for politics, law, business and religion.
forum-valley-temples-basilicas-morning.body: The Roman Forum was a long open space in the valley between the Palatine and Capitoline hills. Originally a marshy area, it had been drained in early times and paved. By 44 before Christ, it was surrounded by temples, law courts and government buildings. The Senate met in the Curia, and speakers addressed the people from a platform called the Rostra, decorated with the bows of captured ships. Large covered halls called basilicas housed courts and business. The Basilica Aemilia and the Basilica Julia, which Caesar had begun, stood on opposite sides. Historians reconstruct the Forum from ancient descriptions and from excavations carried out since the nineteenth century. The ruins can still be visited today. Even so, the Forum changed constantly, as leaders built and rebuilt monuments to display their power. In Caesar's time, it was crowded, noisy and full of life, the meeting place of the whole city.

capitoline-temple-jupiter-gilded-roof-mo.head: On the Capitoline Hill stood the great temple of Jupiter, with a roof of gilded bronze tiles.
capitoline-temple-jupiter-gilded-roof-mo.body: The Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus, meaning Jupiter Best and Greatest, was the most important temple in Rome. It stood on the Capitoline Hill above the Forum and was shared with the goddesses Juno and Minerva. The first temple on the site was traditionally dated to the earliest years of the Republic. It burned down in 83 before Christ and was rebuilt in grand style. The new temple was dedicated in 69 before Christ by Quintus Lutatius Catulus. Its roof was covered with tiles of gilded bronze, which shone in the sun. Historians know about the temple from ancient writers and from the remains of its huge foundations, which can still be seen in Rome. Victorious generals ended their triumphal processions here, offering sacrifices to Jupiter. Even so, the temple was damaged and rebuilt several more times in later centuries. In 44 before Christ, it was the religious heart of the Roman state.

crowded-roman-street-people-many-lands-m.head: Rome was the largest city in the Mediterranean world, with people from many lands speaking many languages.
crowded-roman-street-people-many-lands-m.body: Historians estimate that Rome had perhaps three quarters of a million to a million inhabitants around this time. There was no modern census of the whole population, so the figures are approximate. They are based on records of grain distribution, the size of the city and comparisons with other ancient cities. Rome attracted people from all over the Mediterranean. There were Italians, Greeks, Syrians, Egyptians, Jews, Gauls, Spaniards and many others. Some came as merchants, teachers, doctors or artists. Many others were brought as enslaved people. Latin was the main language, but Greek was widely spoken, especially among educated Romans and immigrants from the eastern Mediterranean. Inscriptions from Rome show names from many regions. Even so, Roman citizens remained a privileged group, and newcomers did not always have the same rights. The mixture of peoples gave the city great variety. Visitors described Rome as the meeting place of the whole world.

grain-ships-harbour-amphorae-unloading.head: Grain from Egypt, Sicily and North Africa, wine from Spain and marble from Greece were shipped to Rome.
grain-ships-harbour-amphorae-unloading.body: Rome had grown rich through centuries of conquest. By 44 before Christ, it controlled Italy, Spain, Greece, much of North Africa, Gaul and lands in the eastern Mediterranean. Goods from all these regions flowed to the capital. Grain arrived from Sicily, Sardinia and North Africa, and increasingly from Egypt. Wine and olive oil came from Spain and Italy, and fine marble from Greece. Most goods arrived by sea at the port of Ostia, at the mouth of the Tiber, and were carried upriver to Rome by barge. Historians study this trade through shipwrecks, writings and the remains of storage jars, called amphorae. Near the river in Rome stands Monte Testaccio, an artificial hill made of millions of broken oil amphorae, mostly from a later period. Even so, the supply system was not always reliable. Storms, pirates and wars could interrupt deliveries. Feeding the huge city remained a constant political concern.

quiet-forum-evening-lamps-few-people-col.head: For about a century before 44 before Christ, Rome had been troubled by political violence and civil wars.
quiet-forum-evening-lamps-few-people-col.body: The late Roman Republic was a period of great instability. From the time of the brothers Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus in the second century before Christ, Roman politics became increasingly violent. Reformers and their opponents were killed in street fighting. In the 80s before Christ, the generals Marius and Sulla fought a civil war, and Sulla published lists of enemies who could be killed and their property seized. Later, the politicians Pompey, Crassus and Caesar formed an informal alliance to share power. Historians call this the First Triumvirate. When it broke down, civil war followed between Caesar and Pompey. Ancient writers such as Sallust, Cicero and later Plutarch and Appian describe these conflicts. Historians debate the causes of the Republic's crisis. Explanations include the power of ambitious generals, the loyalty of soldiers to their commanders, inequality and the difficulty of governing a large empire with city-state institutions. Even so, many Romans still hoped for stability and peace.

julius-caesar-portrait-laurel-wreath-tog.head: Ancient writers reported that Julius Caesar liked to wear a laurel wreath, partly to hide his baldness.
julius-caesar-portrait-laurel-wreath-tog.body: In early 44 before Christ, Gaius Julius Caesar was fifty-five years old. The historian Suetonius, writing about a hundred and fifty years later, described him as tall, with a fair complexion and dark, lively eyes. He was careful about his appearance. Suetonius wrote that Caesar was sensitive about his baldness. He combed his thin hair forward and welcomed the honour of wearing a laurel wreath at all times, which the Senate had granted him. Historians rely on Suetonius, Plutarch and other ancient writers for such personal details, but they treat them with some caution. These authors wrote long after Caesar's death and sometimes included gossip. Portraits of Caesar on coins issued in 44 before Christ show a thin face with a lined neck. Even so, no portrait can be certain. Several marble heads are believed to show Caesar, but scholars disagree about which are most accurate. The image of Caesar has been shaped by centuries of art and legend.

subura-crowded-street-shops-apartments.head: Caesar's family claimed descent from the goddess Venus, yet he grew up in the crowded Subura district.
subura-crowded-street-shops-apartments.body: Caesar was born in Rome in 100 before Christ, into the Julii, an old patrician family. The family claimed descent from Iulus, the son of the Trojan hero Aeneas, and through him from the goddess Venus. Despite this distinguished ancestry, the family was not especially rich or powerful in Caesar's youth. According to Suetonius, Caesar grew up in the Subura, a busy and crowded district of Rome. The Subura lay in a valley northeast of the Forum and was known for its noisy streets, shops and apartment blocks. Historians note that it was a lively, sometimes rough neighbourhood. Caesar later used his family's legendary descent to build his reputation. He dedicated a temple to Venus Genetrix, Venus the Mother, in his new forum. Even so, his childhood among ordinary Romans may have helped him understand the people of the city. His popularity with the urban crowd became an important part of his political success.

roman-matron-mother-teaching-boy-courtya.head: Caesar's mother, Aurelia, raised him after his father's death and remained an important figure in his life.
roman-matron-mother-teaching-boy-courtya.body: Caesar's father, also called Gaius Julius Caesar, died suddenly around 85 before Christ, when his son was about fifteen. Caesar's mother, Aurelia, then took charge of the household. She came from a well-connected family, the Aurelii Cottae. Ancient writers praised her as a strict, intelligent and capable woman. The historian Tacitus later named her as an example of a mother who guided her children's education with great care. Aurelia lived with Caesar for much of her life. When he became chief priest, she lived in his official residence. Historians note that Roman mothers of the upper classes often played important roles in their sons' careers, using family connections and giving advice. Aurelia is also mentioned in the story of a scandal in 62 before Christ, when she discovered a man disguised as a woman at a religious ceremony in Caesar's house. Even so, few details of her life survive. She died in 54 before Christ.

roman-orator-speaking-crowd-forum-rostra.head: Caesar once owed so much money that he could not leave Rome until the wealthy Crassus guaranteed his debts.
roman-orator-speaking-crowd-forum-rostra.body: As a young politician, Caesar spent heavily to win popularity. He paid for public games, entertainments and buildings, and he borrowed large sums to do so. Ancient writers describe him as a brilliant speaker, almost equal to Cicero, and as a clear and elegant writer. His accounts of his wars, the Commentaries on the Gallic War and on the Civil War, are still read today. In 61 before Christ, Caesar was appointed governor of Further Spain. According to Plutarch, his creditors tried to stop him from leaving Rome until his debts were paid. Marcus Licinius Crassus, the richest man in Rome, agreed to guarantee a large part of the debt. Historians note that political careers in the late Republic were extremely expensive. Many politicians borrowed money in the hope of repaying it through a profitable governorship. Even so, Caesar's debts were exceptional. His success in Spain and later in Gaul made him very wealthy.

ancient-pirate-ship-calm-sea-island-coas.head: According to ancient writers, the young Caesar told pirates who captured him that his ransom was too low.
ancient-pirate-ship-calm-sea-island-coas.body: Around 75 before Christ, Caesar sailed to the island of Rhodes to study rhetoric with a famous teacher. On the way, his ship was captured by pirates near the island of Pharmacusa, off the coast of Asia Minor. Plutarch tells that the pirates demanded a ransom of twenty talents. Caesar laughed and said they did not know who they had captured, and offered to pay fifty. He spent about thirty-eight days as their prisoner while his companions collected the money. During this time, he joked with the pirates, wrote poems and speeches, and told them he would have them crucified. After his release, he gathered ships, captured the pirates and carried out his threat. Historians note that piracy was a serious problem in the Mediterranean at the time. Even so, the details of this story come from writers who lived long after the event. It may have been exaggerated to show Caesar's confidence and determination.

domus-publica-house-forum-temple-vesta-r.head: As chief priest of Rome, Caesar lived in an official residence in the Forum called the Domus Publica.
domus-publica-house-forum-temple-vesta-r.body: In 63 before Christ, Caesar was elected Pontifex Maximus, the chief priest of the Roman state religion. This was a position for life and carried great prestige. Caesar was only about thirty-seven years old and faced older, more experienced candidates. According to ancient writers, he borrowed heavily to win the election. The Pontifex Maximus oversaw religious law, the calendar and the Vestal Virgins. He lived in an official house called the Domus Publica, on the Sacred Way in the Forum, next to the House of the Vestals and the Temple of Vesta. Historians note that the position gave Caesar both influence and a prominent home at the centre of the city. Archaeologists have studied the area and identified remains associated with the residence. Even so, the exact layout of the Domus Publica in Caesar's time is uncertain. Caesar continued to hold the office until his death, even while he was away on campaigns.

river-rubicon-small-stream-winter-soldie.head: In January 49 before Christ, Caesar led his army across the Rubicon, a small river, starting a civil war.
river-rubicon-small-stream-winter-soldie.body: The Rubicon was a small river in northern Italy that marked the boundary between the province of Cisalpine Gaul and Italy itself. Roman law forbade a governor to bring his army out of his province into Italy without permission. In January 49 before Christ, Caesar's command in Gaul was coming to an end, and his opponents in the Senate wanted to put him on trial. Rather than give up his army, Caesar crossed the Rubicon with a single legion. According to Suetonius, he said that the die was cast. Historians regard this moment as the start of a civil war. The exact location of the ancient Rubicon is uncertain, because rivers in the area have changed their course. A river in the region was officially named the Rubicone in the twentieth century. Even so, the phrase crossing the Rubicon has become a common expression for passing a point of no return.

caesar-receiving-former-enemies-courtyar.head: Caesar became known for pardoning his defeated enemies, a policy called clementia.
caesar-receiving-former-enemies-courtyar.body: The civil war between Caesar and his opponents lasted from 49 to 45 before Christ and was fought across the Mediterranean. Caesar's great rival, Pompey, was defeated at the Battle of Pharsalus in Greece in 48 before Christ. He fled to Egypt, where he was killed on the orders of advisers to the young king Ptolemy the Thirteenth. Caesar went on to defeat other opponents in Africa and Spain. Unlike earlier leaders such as Sulla, Caesar did not execute large numbers of his enemies. Instead, he pardoned many of them and even gave them positions. This policy became known as Caesar's clemency, or clementia. Historians note that it won Caesar some loyalty but also caused resentment. Some proud nobles disliked owing their lives to his mercy, because it implied that he had power over them. Even so, clemency helped end the war. Several of the men later involved in Caesar's assassination had been pardoned by him.

dawn-roman-street-shutters-opening-shops.head: The Romans divided daylight into twelve hours, so an hour was longer in summer than in winter.
dawn-roman-street-shutters-opening-shops.body: The Roman day began at sunrise. Romans divided the time between sunrise and sunset into twelve equal hours. Because the length of daylight changed through the year, the length of an hour changed too. In midwinter, an hour was about forty-five modern minutes. In midsummer, it was about seventy-five minutes. The night was divided into four watches. Romans measured time with sundials and water clocks. The first sundial in Rome was brought from Sicily in the third century before Christ. Historians note that the timing of daily life followed daylight closely. Shops opened early, and bakers began work before dawn. The poet Martial, writing later, complained about bakers and schoolmasters disturbing his sleep. Even so, most people did not need precise timekeeping. They followed the rhythm of the sun and of public signals, such as announcements in the Forum. The day was busiest in the morning, when most business was done.

roman-school-arcade-children-wax-tablets.head: Roman primary schools often met in open arcades, and neighbours complained about the noise.
roman-school-arcade-children-wax-tablets.body: Education in Rome was private. There was no state school system, and parents paid teachers directly. Children of families who could afford it attended a primary school, called a ludus, from about the age of seven. The teacher, known as a litterator or ludi magister, taught reading, writing and basic arithmetic. Many schools were held in shops or under covered arcades opening onto the street. Pupils wrote on wax tablets with a pointed stylus and recited lessons aloud. Historians know about Roman schools from writers such as Quintilian, Horace and Martial. Martial complained about schoolmasters shouting and beating pupils early in the morning. Discipline was strict, and corporal punishment was common. Even so, education varied greatly. Some children were taught at home by educated slaves or tutors. Many poor children received little or no formal schooling. Literacy levels in Rome are debated by historians, but many people could read at least simple notices.

atrium-clients-waiting-togas-morning-lig.head: Every morning, poorer Romans visited the homes of powerful patrons to greet them in a custom called the salutatio.
atrium-clients-waiting-togas-morning-lig.body: Roman society was organised partly through the relationship between patrons and clients. A patron was a powerful man who offered protection, help and sometimes money. Clients were less powerful citizens who gave support in return, such as votes, loyalty and public attendance. Each morning, clients dressed in their togas and went to the patron's house for the salutatio, or morning greeting. They waited in the entrance hall to pay their respects. The patron received them, sometimes gave them small gifts or food, and listened to requests. Afterwards, clients often accompanied him to the Forum, showing his importance. Historians note that the number of clients reflected a man's status. Writers such as Cicero, and later Martial and Juvenal, describe this custom. Even so, the system was not only about power. Patrons were expected to help clients in legal and personal matters. The relationship was a basic part of Roman life.

atrium-ancestor-masks-shrine-lares-pool.head: Noble Roman families kept wax masks of their ancestors in cupboards in the atrium.
atrium-ancestor-masks-shrine-lares-pool.body: The atrium was the main hall of a traditional Roman house. It had an opening in the roof, called the compluvium, which let in light and rain. Below it was a shallow pool, the impluvium, which collected the water. Around the atrium were doorways to other rooms. In noble families, the atrium displayed the imagines, wax masks of ancestors who had held high office. They were kept in small cupboards, with labels describing each person's achievements. The Greek historian Polybius described how these masks were worn by actors at funerals, so that the ancestors seemed to walk in procession. Historians note that the masks expressed the importance of family history in Roman politics. The household shrine, called the lararium, often stood in or near the atrium. It held images of the household gods, the Lares and Penates. Even so, no Roman ancestor masks have survived. They are known only from written descriptions and some related portraits.

forum-morning-crowds-basilica-arcades-la.head: In the Forum, bankers changed money, lawyers argued cases and crowds gathered to hear news and gossip.
forum-morning-crowds-basilica-arcades-la.body: After the morning greeting, many important Romans went to the Forum with their clients. The Forum was busiest in the morning. In the basilicas, magistrates heard legal cases, and lawyers made speeches before juries and spectators. Bankers and moneychangers worked at tables in arcades near the square. Politicians met supporters, and senators gathered before meetings. Historians know about these activities from the speeches of Cicero, many of which were delivered in the Forum. People also came to hear announcements, read public notices and exchange news. The playwright Plautus, writing more than a century earlier, joked about the different types of people found in different parts of the Forum. In 44 before Christ, a common subject of conversation was Caesar himself, his honours and his plans. Even so, the Forum was also a place of ordinary business. Shopkeepers, vendors and idle onlookers mixed with the powerful and the famous.

roman-street-afternoon-quiet-shade-fount.head: By midday, much of the day's work in Rome was done, and many people rested.
roman-street-afternoon-quiet-shade-fount.body: Roman working days generally started early and ended early. Many public activities, including courts and the Senate, took place in the morning. Around midday, people ate a light meal called the prandium. It might include bread, cheese, olives, fruit, cold meat or leftovers from the previous evening. Afterwards, many Romans rested during the warmest part of the day. This custom was especially common in summer. The word siesta comes from the Latin sexta hora, meaning the sixth hour, which was around noon. Historians note that the afternoon was often spent at the baths, exercising or meeting friends. Letters of Cicero and later writers describe daily routines of this kind. Even so, routines varied greatly by social class. Wealthy Romans had more freedom to rest, while workers, shopkeepers and enslaved people often continued working. In winter, with shorter days, the timetable was more compressed. Streets became quieter in the early afternoon.

dark-roman-street-night-torch-slaves-lig.head: A law of Caesar's banned most heavy carts from the streets of Rome during the day, so wagons moved at night.
dark-roman-street-night-torch-slaves-lig.body: Rome's streets were narrow and crowded. To reduce congestion, a law passed in Caesar's time, recorded in an inscription called the Tabula Heracleensis, banned most wheeled vehicles from the city during the first ten hours of the day. Exceptions were made for carts carrying building materials for temples and public works, and for certain religious ceremonies. As a result, carts delivering goods moved through the city at night. Later writers, especially the poet Juvenal, complained that the noise of wagons made sleep impossible. Historians note that this law is one of the earliest known traffic regulations. At night, the streets had no public lighting. Wealthy people returning from dinner were accompanied by slaves carrying torches. Others carried small oil lamps. Even so, the night streets could be dangerous. Ancient writers mention thieves, falling objects and drunken young men. Most Romans stayed at home after dark and went to bed early.

triclinium-dining-room-painted-walls-thr.head: At a Roman dinner party, guests reclined on three couches arranged around a table, leaning on their left elbows.
triclinium-dining-room-painted-walls-thr.body: The main meal of the day for wealthy Romans was dinner, called the cena. It began in the late afternoon, often after a visit to the baths. Dinner parties were held in a dining room called the triclinium, named after its three couches. Each couch usually held three diners, so the ideal party had nine guests. The couches were arranged in a U shape around a low table, leaving one side open for servants. Guests reclined on their left side, leaning on cushions and eating with their right hand. The seating followed rules of precedence, with places of honour for important guests. Historians know these customs from literature, wall paintings and archaeological remains of dining rooms, especially at Pompeii. Women in Caesar's time often reclined with men at dinner, though customs varied. Even so, most ordinary Romans did not dine this way. They ate simple meals sitting on stools or at home in small apartments.

roman-starters-eggs-olives-oysters-silve.head: A Roman saying described a long dinner as lasting from the egg to the apples.
roman-starters-eggs-olives-oysters-silve.body: A formal Roman dinner had three main parts. First came the gustatio, or starters. These could include eggs, olives, lettuce, mushrooms, shellfish, small salted fish and sausages. Diners often drank mulsum, a mixture of wine and honey. Next came the main courses, with meat, poultry and fish. Pork was especially popular, along with game, ducks and fish from the sea and rivers. Finally came dessert, called secundae mensae, meaning second tables, with fruit, nuts and sweet cakes. Because meals often began with eggs and ended with apples, the poet Horace used the phrase ab ovo usque ad mala, from the egg to the apples, meaning from beginning to end. Historians know about Roman food from writers, from a later cookbook attributed to Apicius and from archaeological remains of food. Even so, such dinners were for the wealthy. Most Romans ate much simpler meals of grain, vegetables and a little meat or fish.

clay-amphorae-garum-jars-kitchen-shelf-h.head: Romans flavoured many dishes with garum, a sauce made from fermented fish.
clay-amphorae-garum-jars-kitchen-shelf-h.body: Garum was one of the most popular flavourings in Roman cooking. It was made by layering small fish, such as anchovies or mackerel, with salt in large containers and leaving them in the sun for weeks or months. The fish broke down and fermented, producing a salty liquid. This liquid was strained and stored in amphorae. Garum was used in many dishes, both savoury and sweet. Historians note that the process was smelly, so production often took place outside towns. Large garum factories have been found along the coasts of Spain, North Africa and Portugal. Garum from certain places was highly prized and expensive. Cheaper versions, often called liquamen, were used by ordinary people. Even so, the flavour of garum may have been less strong than its method suggests. Modern experiments suggest that it tasted similar to fish sauces used in Southeast Asian cooking today. It added a rich, savoury taste to Roman food.

roman-dessert-figs-grapes-honey-cakes-la.head: Roman dinners had no forks, tomatoes, potatoes or sugar.
roman-dessert-figs-grapes-honey-cakes-la.body: Many foods common today were unknown in ancient Rome. Tomatoes, potatoes, maize, peppers and chocolate all came from the Americas and reached Europe only in the sixteenth century. Sugar was known only as a rare medicine from India. Instead, Romans sweetened their food with honey and with grape syrups. Desserts included apples, pears, figs, grapes, dates, nuts, cheese and cakes made with honey. Diners ate with their fingers, spoons and knives. Forks were not used for eating in ancient Rome, though larger forks were used in kitchens. Napkins were used to wipe hands, and guests sometimes took food home wrapped in them. Historians use ancient texts and archaeological evidence, such as seeds and bones found at Roman sites, to reconstruct the diet. Even so, the Roman diet was varied and sophisticated for the wealthy. It included many herbs and spices, such as pepper imported from India, which was very popular.

musician-lyre-playing-dinner-guests-list.head: Guests at Roman dinner parties were entertained by music, poetry readings, conversation and performers.
musician-lyre-playing-dinner-guests-list.body: Entertainment was an important part of Roman dinner parties. Musicians played the lyre or double pipes. Educated slaves might read poetry or literature aloud. Dancers, singers and acrobats sometimes performed. Witty conversation was highly valued, and hosts aimed to bring together interesting guests. Some Romans disapproved of extravagant entertainments and preferred quiet discussions of philosophy or literature. Cicero's writings describe dinners filled with conversation about politics and books. Historians note that dinner parties were also occasions for building political alliances and friendships. The poet Horace and later the writer Pliny the Younger described their ideal dinners, with simple food and good company. Even so, some dinners were known for excess. Later satirists, such as Petronius, mocked wealthy hosts who displayed their riches in vulgar ways. In Caesar's time, dinner parties reflected the host's taste and status. They could last for many hours, often into the night.

seaside-villa-dinner-winter-evening-gues.head: In December 45 before Christ, Caesar visited Cicero's villa near the sea, accompanied by about two thousand soldiers.
seaside-villa-dinner-winter-evening-gues.body: One of Cicero's letters describes a visit from Caesar in December 45 before Christ. Caesar was travelling along the coast of Campania, near the Bay of Naples, and stopped at Cicero's villa near Puteoli. He came with a large escort, which Cicero estimated at about two thousand soldiers. Cicero worried about where they would all stay. Caesar spent the morning at a neighbour's house, then bathed and dined with Cicero. Cicero wrote to his friend Atticus that the dinner went well. The conversation was pleasant and avoided politics, focusing mainly on literature. He added that Caesar was not the kind of guest to whom one says, please come again. Historians value this letter for its personal, humorous view of Caesar only a few months before his death. Even so, it also shows the tension between the two men. Cicero was polite, but he did not support Caesar's political dominance. The letter survives among Cicero's correspondence to Atticus.
